newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek government turns down farmers' truce offer.
newsitem.headline: Greek government turns down farmers' truce offer.

text.p: Greece's embattled socialist government on Thursday snubbed an olive branch offered by protesting farmers, who asked to meet Prime Minister Costas Simitis and vowed not to block roads for the day.
The government, which has faced an almost constant wave of strikes and protests against its strict ecomomic policies since coming to power in September, said it would not accept an ultimatum.
"All forms of mobilisation and threats to close off the roads must clearly stop for such a meeting to be possible," government spokesman Dimitris Reppas told reporters.
The farmers gave Simitis until Thursday night to say whether he will meet them, otherwise they would take over major highways with their tractors.
"The aim is to begin a dialogue with the prime minister. It all depends on him now. We're waiting for his move," farmers' representative Thanassis Nassikas told television.

Farmers in central Greece have been playing a hide-and-seek game with police for the past three days, driving their tractors off the roads and across vast farmlands or under bridges whenever riot squads and police helicopters confronted them.

They briefly blocked minor roads in a bid to show that the thousands of police -- many in riot gear -- dispatched to the area could not stop them from repeating a crippling road blockade that virtually cut the country in two in December.
"We can go anywhere we want and no one can stop us but we are not blocking roads," Nassikas said.
Simitis successfully waited out that 25-day blockade, saying the country could not afford to satisfy their demands, which include cheaper fuel, lower taxes and more subsidies.
The farmers gave up the December blockade because of the Christmas holidays but vowed to bring their tractors back to highways if their demands were not met.
They are among a long list of groups protesting or striking against a 1997 budget described as the toughest in 15 years, and strict incomes and tax policies.
Teachers are on strike for a third week while labour confederations have staged repeated walkouts against the government. Protest rallies almost daily congest traffic in the Greek capital.
Simitis has icely turned down all labour demands, saying giving in would risk Greece's efforts to catch up with its European Union partners.
But the confrontation with the farmers seems to have at last ruffled his feathers.
On Wednesday he cancelled a planned meeting of the Panhellenic Socialist Movement central committee on the farmers issue for fear of criticism from within his own party, government officials said.

Instead of the meeting, which was due Friday and Saturday but will be held on February 21-22, government ministers and senior party officials will be sent to the countryside over the weekend to placade the farmers, the officials said.
